All 20 tech stocks on a list from financial newsletter The Kobeissi Letter trade at least 25% below record highs. CoreWeave (CRWV) leads the slide at 76%.

Additionally, the S&P 500 has lost over $6 trillion in six weeks adding pressure to the markets in general. The Nasdaq Composite, however, sits in correction territory, a 10% decline, not the 20% that defines a bear market.

Why Are Cloud and Chip Names Falling Hardest?

The deepest drops cluster in cloud computing, chips, and data storage. Oracle (ORCL) and SanDisk (SNDK), a flash memory maker, each trail their highs by 68%. Nebius (NBIS), an artificial intelligence (AI) cloud provider, is down 66%.

Intel (INTC) is down 61%. Western Digital (WDC), a data storage maker, and Arm (ARM), a chip designer, each trail by 60%. Tesla (TSLA) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) show the mildest declines at 25%, still beyond the 20% bear market line.

CoreWeave, which rents computing capacity to AI developers, grew third-quarter revenue 168% to $3.66 billion. Its net loss still reached $709 million, with net interest expense at $846 million, according to its results.

A correction means a 10% decline from a record, while a bear market requires 20%. The Nasdaq Composite closed at 23,879.20 on Nov. 19. That sits below the 24,315.00 close that confirmed its correction on Nov. 5, CNBC reported.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 fell 2.02% on Nov. 19 to 7,175.83. AMD fell further after short seller Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a bet against the chipmaker.

Will the Indexes Follow These Tech Stocks Lower?

The Kobeissi Letter, meanwhile, has described the selloff as a historic opportunity. In both earlier 2026 episodes, in March and July, the Composite later set new records, a Motley Fool analysis shows.

If that pattern holds, indexes could recover while these 20 stocks lag. A close 20% below the Oct. 6 record, however, would most likely break it.

Intuit (INTU) came out with quarterly earnings of $2.91 per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $2.46 per share. This compares to earnings of $3.34 per share a year ago. These figures are adjusted for non-recurring items.

This quarterly report represents an earnings surprise of +18.29%. A quarter ago, it was expected that this maker of TurboTax, QuickBooks and other accounting software would post earnings of $3.59 per share when it actually produced earnings of $4.03, delivering a surprise of +12.26%.

Over the last four quarters, the company has surpassed consensus EPS estimates four times.

Intuit, which belongs to the Zacks Computer - Software industry, posted revenues of $4.35 billion for the quarter ended October 2026, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 1.14%. This compares to year-ago revenues of $3.89 billion. The company has topped consensus revenue estimates four times over the last four quarters.

The sustainability of the stock's immediate price movement based on the recently-released numbers and future earnings expectations will mostly depend on management's commentary on the earnings call.

Intuit shares have lost about 52.7% since the beginning of the year versus the S&P 500's gain of 7%.

What's Next for Intuit?

While Intuit has underperformed the market so far this year, the question that comes to investors' minds is: what's next for the stock?

There are no easy answers to this key question, but one reliable measure that can help investors address this is the company's earnings outlook. Not only does this include current consensus earnings expectations for the coming quarter(s), but also how these expectations have changed lately.

Empirical research shows a strong correlation between near-term stock movements and trends in earnings estimate revisions. Investors can track such revisions by themselves or rely on a tried-and-tested rating tool like the Zacks Rank, which has an impressive track record of harnessing the power of earnings estimate revisions.

Ahead of this earnings release, the estimate revisions trend for Intuit was mixed. While the magnitude and direction of estimate revisions could change following the company's just-released earnings report, the current status translates into a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) for the stock. So, the shares are expected to perform in line with the market in the near future. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here.

It will be interesting to see how estimates for the coming quarters and the current fiscal year change in the days ahead. The current consensus EPS estimate is $3.70 on $5.15 billion in revenues for the coming quarter and $23.47 on $23.39 billion in revenues for the current fiscal year.

A record quarter at CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) has clashed with mounting concerns about its debt. CoreWeave stock is down 25% over the past month to $46.04 in afternoon trading. That slide includes a 4% drop from the prior close, leaving the AI cloud provider caught between booming demand and a heavy financing bill.

24/7 Wall St.

The 52-week range for CoreWeave runs from a low of $40.58 to a high of $138.25. With the share price now between $40 and $50, the question for shareholders is which level CoreWeave reaches first. Both paths find real support in the company's latest numbers.

Debt and Spending Put $40 in Play for CoreWeave

On top of that, CoreWeave expects full-year 2026 capital expenditures of $37 billion to $39 billion.

Profit taking across AI stocks around the November 19 market debut of Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) adds pressure on CoreWeave. CEO Michael Intrator canceled his Rule 10b5-1 trading plan, a prearranged stock-sale schedule, after CoreWeave's Q3 report.

Today's big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?

For most of the last 15 years, the best thing about owning Big Tech was its cash. That cash paid for dividends and for buybacks, when a company buys back its own shares. It bought rivals. It carried these companies through 2020 and 2022.

That is why many investors treat Microsoft or Alphabet almost like a bond. In 2026, the cash is going somewhere else. This is the first follow-up to our cash series hub, What If Google Slows Its $160 Billion AI Spend?

The short answer: five of the biggest AI builders now put most of their cash into capital spending. That is money spent on long-lived assets such as data centers. Two of the five spend more than all of their cash. In 2023, they had $213 billion of free cash flow between them, the cash left after capital spending. Over the last year, they had $33 billion.

How Much Of Their Cash Goes Into Building?

Most of it. For two of them, more than all of it. The five are Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, Amazon and Oracle. Amazon spent $1.28 on capital spending for every $1 of cash its business brought in. Oracle spent $1.61. Ten years ago, the highest of the five was Amazon, at 41 cents.

Meanwhile, the Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500's, from 50 stocks with at least 10 straight years of dividends. See what it pays.

What Did Cash Buy Them Before?

Trust. Alphabet bought back $61.5 billion of its own stock in 2023 and $62.2 billion in 2024. Oracle bought back $21.6 billion in its 2021 fiscal year. Buybacks like these told investors the company had more cash than it could use. In our view, that promise was part of what investors paid for, as much as any product.

What Has Changed?

Oracle's buybacks fell from $21.6 billion to $0.2 billion. That is about $200 million, in its fiscal year to May 2026. Alphabet's buybacks fell to $45.7 billion in 2025, from $62.2 billion. That year, its capital spending rose 74%.

Some of the cash that used to buy back stock now buys into the AI race itself. Nvidia and Google are among the buyers of Anthropic's shares alongside its IPO.

Today's big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?

A year ago, Alphabet owed $26.6 billion. Now it owes $126.1 billion. It is not the only AI builder borrowing this way.

When a company spends more than its business brings in, the gap has to be paid for. For the AI builders in 2026, the money came mostly from lenders. This piece is part of our cash series. The series starts with What If Google Slows Its $160 Billion AI Spend?

The short answer: five of the biggest builders added $306 billion of debt in a year. All of the new borrowing came from Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle. They kept borrowing as the 10-year Treasury yield rose past 5%. It was last that high in 2007.

Who Borrowed The Most?

Amazon did. Its debt rose by $125 billion and more than tripled, to $180.3 billion. Alphabet's debt nearly quintupled, to $126 billion. That is nearly $100 billion of new borrowing in a single year. Meta's debt nearly tripled, to $83.7 billion. Microsoft went the other way and cut its debt.

Can Alphabet borrow another $100 billion? In our view, it likely can. What matters is what each new dollar costs.

Debt here means borrowed money only: notes, loans and commercial paper, which is short-term IOUs. Leases are not included.

Oracle's side of the story is in Why Is Oracle Spending $1.61 For Every Cash Dollar?

Four of these five leaders borrowed heavily in one year, and one cut its debt. If you like companies like these, you do not have to pick just one. The Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio holds 30 quality companies in equal weight, and has returned more than 105% since its September 2020 launch. Look inside HQ.

What Does That Money Cost?

About eight times as much as in 2020, by the base rate.

The 10-year Treasury yield is the base rate for long-term company borrowing. In August 2020, it averaged 0.65%. In October 2026, it averaged 5.13%. It was last this high in 2007.

Big Tech pays more than that rate when it borrows. So every new dollar of debt now carries interest that a 2020 borrower barely paid. Cash used to be nearly free for these companies. Now it has a price.

Is It Only The Public Companies?

No. Anthropic raised $110.7 billion from financing in the first nine months of 2026. Over the same months, its business brought in $6.6 billion of cash. It put $36.5 billion into investments, mostly short-term securities such as Treasuries.

title: Why CoreWeave Can't Pay Down Debt From Its Cash

CoreWeave does not pay for its growth from its own cash, let alone pay down its debt. Over the four quarters to September 2026, it spent $27.6 billion on equipment and buildings. That spending is called capital spending, or capex. The cash its business brought in, called operating cash flow, covered only 26.1% of it.

The stock closed at $47.83 on Wednesday, Nov 18, down 4.1%. That was the day after Nvidia reported, and Nvidia itself fell 2.9%. CoreWeave has lost 21.3% since its jump on Nov 11. Our sources do not record a cause for Wednesday's drop.

Two similar AI cloud companies, Nebius and IREN, fail the same test. Their operating cash flow covered 29.0% and 27.5% of their capex, in that order. The difference lies in how they filled the gap and how much cash they hold.

Where Did CoreWeave's Money Come From?

Most of it was borrowed. Net new borrowing, meaning new debt minus debt repaid, equalled 84.5% of capex. Selling new shares added another 10.8%. Cash from the business filled only about a quarter of the bill. Together, the three sources came to more than capex, so some of the money went to other uses or stayed as cash.

Most of CoreWeave's growth runs on borrowed money, not on cash its business brings in. For your own money, cash that comes in steadily can matter more than fast growth. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500's, and it lost less than the S&P 500 in all 9 big selloffs since 2018. See the metrics.

So the debt grew fast. CoreWeave's total debt rose from $18.8 billion to $66.2 billion in the year to Sep 30. That figure includes $19.3 billion of lease obligations. At Wednesday's close, the debt was about 2.5 times the company's stock market value of $26.5 billion.

Can CoreWeave Cover The Debt Due Within A Year?

Not from cash on hand. CoreWeave held $4.1 billion of cash on Sep 30. It had $10.6 billion of debt due within a year. We think that means it needs new loans or other outside money to meet those payments.

The interest bill is also heavy. Interest expense came to $2.4 billion over the four quarters. That equals 24.4% of revenue. Operating cash flow was about 3.0 times that interest expense.

So CoreWeave can pay its interest from its own cash. It cannot pay down the debt that way while it keeps building at this pace.

Today's big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?

Nvidia's neocloud customers cannot pay for their chips from their own cash. Neoclouds are young companies that rent out AI computing power. Over the four quarters to September 2026, CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN spent $54.2 billion on data centers and equipment. That spending is called capital spending, or capex.

Their operating cash flow is the cash their businesses brought in. It covered only 27.2% of that capex. The other $39.4 billion came from outside money. That means new debt, leases or new shares. In our view, every further Nvidia chip order from these three depends on that money staying available.

The neoclouds have fallen far from their highs. At Wednesday's close, CoreWeave was 65.3% below its 52-week high. Nebius was 62.7% below its high. IREN was 77.5% below. This article asks a different question. Who pays Nvidia?

How did these stocks trade after Nvidia's report?

Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the quarter ended Oct 25. That was up 103% from a year earlier. The results came out on Tuesday, Nov 17, after the close. On Wednesday, the first session to trade on them, Nvidia fell 2.9%. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF slipped 0.31%.

CoreWeave fell 4.1% on Wednesday and closed at $47.83. That left it down 21.3% from its Nov 11 close. IREN fell 3.6%. Nebius rose 0.9%.

CoreWeave has lost 21.3% in a week and sits 65.3% below its high. If swings like this make you nervous, income that keeps arriving can make the wait easier. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500's, and it lost less than the S&P 500 in all 9 big selloffs since 2018. See the metrics.

Can the neoclouds fund their spending from their own cash?

No. Each of the three covered less than a third of its capex with operating cash flow. CoreWeave covered 26.1%. Nebius covered 29.0%. IREN covered 27.5%.

Cash on hand does not fill the gap for long. Take each company's shortfall from July to September 2026, meaning capex minus operating cash flow. At that pace, CoreWeave's cash would last about 0.6 of a quarter. IREN's would last about 0.8 of a quarter. Nebius's would last about one quarter.

Nebius also had a weak quarter for cash. Its operating cash flow from July to September was negative. Cash flowed out of the business instead of in.

David Tepper and 27 Other Big Funds Bought Oracle Last Quarter, While 12 Sold. Who's Right? ©@Angelo Dee from ภาพของSakorn Sukkasemsakorn via Canva, @aukidphumsirichat via Canva
Key Takeaways

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 28 bought Oracle and 12 sold. David Tepper's Appaloosa was among the buyers, and Pentwater Capital built a $1.61 billion stake.

Four of the sellers bought Meta Platforms in the same quarter. Meta is another heavy AI spender, with a fast-growing ad business behind it.

Oracle trades at 13x forward earnings against a five-year average of 21x, and analysts expect its earnings to climb through fiscal 2028.

The numbers favor the buyers. But Oracle is funding its AI build with debt, as CoreWeave is, and S&P puts OpenAI at about half of Oracle's backlog.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) is 54% below its 52-week high, and the big funds can't agree on what that means.

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 28 bought Oracle by opening a position or adding 20% or more to one. Twelve sold out or cut 20% or more, and 74 held it at the quarter's end. The counts cover funds readers know by name and funds with $1 billion or more of US stocks in their 13Fs. Quant and index funds are left out.

TIKR tracks 42 analysts on Oracle. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Oracle, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Oracle's Analyst Ratings

Tepper has company, and Pentwater went biggest

David Tepper's Appaloosa opened a position of 1.25 million shares, worth $172 million at Sept. 30. That's from its 13F for the quarter, filed Nov. 16. The stake is 2.3% of its 13F stocks and its 13th-largest holding.

The biggest buy by far came from Pentwater Capital Management, which manages $19 billion. Its 13F, filed the same day, shows its stake growing from 90,000 shares to 11.75 million. Those shares were worth $1.61 billion, or 12.3% of its 13F stocks, making Oracle its second-largest position. Pentwater also reported put options with a notional value of $656 million and call options with a notional value of $323 million. Its 13F doesn't show how the shares and options fit together.

GQG Partners, which manages $164 billion, opened a position of 2.49 million shares worth $341 million, though that's just 0.6% of its 13F stocks. Larry Robbins' Glenview Capital and Jeremy Grantham's GMO opened smaller positions, worth about $74 million and $26 million at quarter-end prices.

Parnassus and Polen did most of the selling

None of the sellers is a famous name. Parnassus Investments, which manages $41 billion, cut its stake 79%, from 2.08 million shares to 439,170. That's about $225 million of stock at quarter-end prices. Polen Capital, which manages $24 billion, sold about $145 million in a 29% cut. Its remaining 2.52 million shares, worth $346 million, are still 3.8% of its 13F stocks. Blue Sparrow, whose 13F holds $8.3 billion of US stocks, cut its stake 94%.
